opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, looking back, I think it was one of those decisions that felt much bigger at the time than it actually was, but it also shaped me in ways I didn't fully appreciate until later.

At that age, the gaokao feels like the whole world. Everyone around you is preparing for it, and there's this sense that it's the one test that defines you. So when the chance for early admission came up, part of me felt relief, and part of me felt almost a little guilty, like I was skipping a rite of passage that all my classmates were going through.

But what it really gave me was time. Instead of spending those last months drilling exam questions, I had space to be curious. I could read things that weren't on any syllabus, play around with computers and programming, and just explore without a clear goal. I think that kind of unstructured time is actually really rare, and really valuable, especially when you're young.

I wouldn't say it was some brilliant strategic choice. I was a teenager; I didn't have a grand plan for becoming a researcher. It was more that the opportunity was there, and it seemed reasonable to take it. In hindsight, though, I think a lot of my later path came from that same instinct: when there's a chance to step a little outside the standard track and have more freedom to follow what interests you, take it. That's been true for me in research, too. Some of the most meaningful work comes from not doing exactly what everyone else is optimizing for.

So overall, I'm grateful for it. I don't think it made me better than anyone who took the gaokao, but it gave me a slightly different starting point, and a bit more room to figure out what I actually cared about.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time it didn't feel like a huge decision. I was in high school, I'd done reasonably well in some competitions, and the opportunity came up to get in through early admission. The alternative was spending another year grinding for the gaokao, and I think most people in my position would have taken the offer. So I did.

Looking back, I think the main thing it gave me was time. Not time in the sense of skipping a year, but mental space. When you're preparing for the gaokao, everything narrows down to one exam, and you optimize everything around that. Once that pressure was off, I actually had a stretch of several months where I could read whatever I wanted, play around with programming, just be curious without a scoreboard. That sounds small, but I think it shaped how I relate to learning. I started to see it as something I did because I found it interesting, rather than because I had to perform.

The other thing I'd say is that it was my first real experience of being evaluated on something other than a standardized test. Early admission looked at a different set of signals, and I remember thinking, okay, there are multiple paths to the same place. That idea stayed with me. In research, there's no single exam you pass. You have to figure out what's worth working on, and that requires a kind of comfort with ambiguity that the gaokao system doesn't really train you for.

Of course, I don't want to romanticize it. I missed out on the shared experience that almost everyone in China goes through, and sometimes when friends talk about it, I do feel a bit like an outsider. And I'm sure I would have been fine if I'd taken the exam. But if you ask whether I regret it, no. It put me at Jiao Tong, in a good environment, a little earlier and a little more relaxed than I otherwise would have been. Everything that came after, including going abroad for graduate school, really built on that starting point.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think it was a choice to accept a good opportunity rather than keep pursuing an uncertain outcome. The gaokao would have been another path, but I already had the opportunity to go to Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and I chose to take it.

Of course, you can always ask what might have happened if you’d made a different decision. I don’t think there’s a way to answer that. What matters more is what you do after making the choice—what you explore, what you learn, and how willing you are to change direction. I wouldn’t attribute everything that came afterward to that one decision.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I think it was a good decision for me, but I wouldn’t turn it into a general prescription. At that age, it’s hard to know exactly what you want, and accepting early admission meant choosing a concrete opportunity over the uncertainty of the gaokao. I don’t think there’s much value in imagining what score I might have gotten or which other university I might have attended. The more useful question is what you do with the opportunity once you’re there.
